article.title: Why a High Average Can Hide a Weak Median Customer
article.why: 避免平均值掩蓋典型顧客與分布的真實變化。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
A rising average can create a comforting story about customer growth. If average annual spend moves from $500 to $620, a team may conclude that customers are becoming more valuable. That conclusion may be correct, but the average alone cannot tell us whether the typical customer improved. A small number of very large customers can pull the mean upward while most customers stay flat or even decline.

Consider 100 customers. Ninety of them spend about $500, while ten spend $5,000. If the ten largest customers increase their spend sharply, the overall average rises even if the other ninety do not change. The business has more revenue, which is good, but it has not necessarily strengthened the behavior of its broad customer base.

The median gives a different view. It is the value in the middle after customers are ordered by spend. Because extreme values have less influence on it, the median can help answer a practical question: what happened to a typical customer? If the mean rises 20 percent but the median rises only 1 percent, the gap deserves investigation.

That does not mean the median is always better. A business may care greatly about high-value customers, and revenue is additive. Losing a customer who spends one million dollars can matter far more than losing a customer who spends one hundred dollars. The point is to match the metric to the question instead of treating one summary statistic as the whole distribution.

A useful analysis therefore combines several views. Start with mean and median spend. Then examine percentiles such as P25, P75, and P90. Look at the share of total revenue contributed by the top 1, 5, or 10 percent of customers. Finally, plot or tabulate the distribution so that shifts in different parts of the customer base are visible.

Time comparisons require another check: customer composition. Suppose this year's customer population contains more premium members than last year's population. The average can rise because the mix changed, even if spending within each membership tier fell. Segment-level comparisons can separate within-group behavioral change from a change in the weights of groups.

For decision making, translate the distribution into business questions. Did more customers cross a meaningful annual-spend threshold? Is growth broad-based or concentrated? Are middle customers moving upward? Has dependence on a small set of heavy spenders increased? These questions often matter more than whether the mean is statistically higher.

A good dashboard can show the mean without letting it dominate the story. Put the median beside it, add a few percentiles, and include a concentration measure. If possible, show the same metrics for important segments and for a stable cohort of customers observed in both periods.

The lesson is not “never use averages.” Averages are useful, easy to compare, and directly related to total value. The lesson is that an average compresses a distribution into one number. When the distribution is skewed, that compression can hide the part of the customer population that a product, loyalty, or marketing team actually wants to change.

For loyalty programs, this distinction can change action. If only the top tail improved, the next campaign may focus on concentration risk or retention of heavy users. If the median and middle percentiles improved together, the evidence is stronger that the broader proposition is working. Distribution-aware measurement therefore connects descriptive statistics directly to strategy.
